title: 1.3 Million TPS Holders Face Work Permit Deadline as Supreme Court Clears Path for Mass Terminations
excerpt: Work permits for Haitians expire July 24, with six other nationalities already past their deadlines, after the Supreme Court's June 25 ruling allowed the Trump administration to end Temporary Protected Status.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • 330,000 Haitian TPS holders face work permit expiration on July 24, impacting various industries.
  • Supreme Court's 6-3 ruling limits judicial review of DHS decisions on Temporary Protected Status.
  • Trump administration seeks to overturn protections for 600,000 Venezuelan TPS holders using the ruling.
  • Labor groups warn mass terminations could disrupt healthcare, construction, and hospitality sectors.
  • Communities are urging legislative action to extend TPS protections amid looming deadlines.

  • Work permits for approximately 330,000 Haitian TPS holders expire July 24, with permits for nationals of Syria, Burma, Ethiopia, Somalia, South Sudan, and Yemen already past their deadline.
  • The Supreme Court ruled 6-3 on June 25 that federal law bars judicial review of non-constitutional challenges to DHS decisions to end Temporary Protected Status.
  • The Trump administration is now using the ruling to push the Supreme Court to overturn a separate appeals court decision protecting 600,000 Venezuelan TPS holders.
  • Labor groups and immigration advocates warn the mass termination could disrupt key industries including healthcare, construction, and hospitality.

The Countdown

For approximately 1.3 million immigrants shielded from deportation under Temporary Protected Status, a Supreme Court ruling last month has turned legal uncertainty into an approaching cliff. Work permits for Haitian TPS holders — roughly 330,000 people — expire July 24. For nationals of Syria, Burma, Ethiopia, Somalia, South Sudan, and Yemen, the deadline has already passed.

The U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services issued a brief reprieve on July 10, extending Haitian work authorization by two weeks and giving nationals of the other six countries until July 17. But those extensions were measured in days, not months, and the underlying legal reality remains unchanged.

"On Thursday, when the Supreme Court made that decision to terminate TPS, they did not just affect Haitians. They put the lives of 1.5 million TPS recipients at risk."

— Tessa Petit, Executive Director, Florida Immigrant Coalition

What the Supreme Court Decided

On June 25, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that the statute governing TPS "plainly bars" judicial review of non-constitutional challenges to the Department of Homeland Security's decision to end humanitarian protections. The case centered on former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem's determination that Haiti and Syria were stable enough to accept returning nationals — a conclusion challenged by advocates who pointed to the State Department's own "Do Not Travel" advisory for Haiti, citing widespread gang violence, kidnappings, and limited healthcare.

The court rejected the argument that Trump's decision was motivated by racial animus. Plaintiffs had cited Trump's baseless claims during the 2024 campaign that Haitian immigrants in Ohio were eating their neighbors' pets.

The Ripple Effect

The ruling's impact extends well beyond Haiti and Syria. On July 9, the Justice Department filed a petition asking the Supreme Court to use its TPS decision to overturn a Ninth Circuit ruling that had protected approximately 600,000 Venezuelan TPS holders. The 9th Circuit had found in January that Noem exceeded her authority in ending Venezuela's TPS designation, but the administration argues the June 25 precedent should vacate that ruling.

For employers, the cascading deadlines create immediate practical problems. Labor groups had urged extensions, arguing that abruptly removing work authorization for over a million workers would cause "chaos in workplaces and disrupt key industries." TPS holders are concentrated in healthcare, construction, food processing, and hospitality — sectors already facing labor shortages.

Communities Brace for Impact

In Springfield, Ohio, home to a significant Haitian community that became the center of national controversy during the 2024 campaign, the looming deadline has shifted conversations from legal arguments to practical survival. Immigration attorneys are advising TPS holders to explore every alternative path to legal status — asylum applications, family-based petitions, employer sponsorship — while acknowledging that most options are slow, expensive, and uncertain.

In Southwest Florida, where an estimated 40,000 TPS holders live, community leaders gathered in Miami in late June to call for legislative action. Advocates are urging the Senate to pass S. 4814, a bill that would designate Haiti for TPS through early 2029.

"Rulings like these aren't just felt in a courtroom. They're felt at kitchen tables, in our churches, in our workplaces," said Vanessa Joseph, an immigration attorney and chair of the National Haitian American Elected Officials Network.

What Comes Next

Lower courts are in the process of issuing final orders to formally terminate TPS as directed by the Supreme Court. Until those orders are entered, the precise timeline for enforcement remains unclear. But the trajectory is unmistakable: the administration has the legal green light to end protections for TPS holders from all designated countries, and it is moving to use it.

For TPS holders whose work authorization has expired or will expire in days, the immediate question is stark: continue working without authorization and risk arrest, or stop working and lose the ability to support their families. Congress could intervene with legislation, but no bill has advanced past committee in either chamber.

The approximately 800,000 Indian nationals on various temporary work visas in the United States are watching these developments closely. While TPS and employment-based visas operate under different legal frameworks, the Supreme Court's deference to executive authority on immigration status sends a broader signal about the limits of judicial protection for immigrants in the current political environment.
